title: India's pavilion wins the Venice Biennale's public vote for best national participation
dek: 'Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home', India's first pavilion in Venice since 2019, took the new Visitors' Lion, created after the jury resigned in April.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
India's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale, "Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home", has won the Visitors' Lion for Best National Participation, La Biennale di Venezia announced on 25 November, three days after the exhibition closed. The American artist Nick Cave won the other Visitors' Lion, for Best Participant in the main exhibition, "In Minor Keys".

The prizes were decided by the public. Only ticket holders who had visited both of the Biennale's main venues, the Giardini and the Arsenale, between 9 May and 22 November could vote, according to the Biennale. It did not publish vote totals.

## The pavilion

India's pavilion, at the Arsenale, was India's first national participation in Venice since 2019. It was commissioned by the National Gallery of Modern Art under the Ministry of Culture, with the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts as the executing agency, and curated by Amin Jaffer.

It showed five artists: Alwar Balasubramaniam, who works in earth and clay; Sumakshi Singh, who made a stitched recreation of her demolished childhood home; Ranjani Shettar, with hanging plant-like forms; Skarma Sonam Tashi from Ladakh, with papier-mâché buildings; and Asim Waqif, who builds with cane and bamboo. The works dealt with memory, migration, materials and the meaning of home, drawing on landscapes from Ladakh to Tamil Nadu, according to reports.

About 4.5 lakh people visited the pavilion, placing it among the most visited national pavilions of this edition, according to the Ministry of Culture, as cited in reports.

Sachchidanand Joshi, member secretary of the IGNCA, said the award was "particularly gratifying" because it reflected the voices of visitors from around the world, according to reports. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Culture Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat both welcomed the win.

## Why a public vote

The Visitors' Lions were introduced this year after all five members of the Biennale's international jury resigned in April, leaving the exhibition without its usual Golden and Silver Lions, according to reports. The jury had objected to exhibits from Russia and Israel, which had been controversial since before the opening, and had signalled it would not give awards to countries whose heads of state have been indicted by the International Criminal Court, according to reports.

The new prizes have their critics. More than half of the individual artists in the main exhibition said they would decline a Visitors' Lion, according to reports. La Biennale's president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, said in announcing the winners that "a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it", a remark he attributed to Pablo Picasso's practice.

## Background

The Venice Biennale, founded in 1895, is the oldest and most prominent international art exhibition. Countries present national pavilions alongside a central exhibition chosen by an artistic director; this year's main show, "In Minor Keys", was conceived by the late curator Koyo Kouoh. India first had a national pavilion in Venice in 2011 and has taken part only intermittently since.

## What happens next

The Biennale's next art exhibition is due in 2028; next year's edition in Venice is the architecture exhibition. Whether India returns with a pavilion will be a decision for the Ministry of Culture.
